name: history_set2_p1
label: History: set 2 (jihads, partition, colonial rule, resistance, nationalism, Pan-Africanism, 20th-century Africa)

papers.title: The 19th Century Jihads: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the 19th century jihads, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The Sokoto jihad of 1804 was led by
questions.explanation:
Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar in Gobir, declared the jihad in 1804 after his hijra to Gudu, and founded the Sokoto Caliphate.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- al-Hajj Umar Tall: al-Hajj Umar led the Tukulor jihad from 1852.
- Seku Ahmadu: Seku Ahmadu led the Masina jihad from 1818.
- Samori Toure: Samori built the Mandinka empire and resisted the French; he did not lead the Sokoto jihad.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a cause of the Sokoto jihad?
questions.explanation:
Causes included religious impurity, oppression and corruption of Hausa rulers, heavy taxes such as the cattle tax, injustice, Fulani grievances and the example of earlier jihads.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the arrival of the Portuguese at Elmina: Elmina was built in 1482 on the coast, far from Hausaland.
- the Berlin Conference's decisions: The Berlin Conference was held in 1884–85.
- British demands for the Golden Stool: That caused the Asante war of 1900.

options.label: A
options.content: the arrival of the Portuguese at Elmina

options.label: C
options.content: Hausa rulers mixing Islam with traditional religious practices

options.label: D
options.content: British demands for the Golden Stool

questions.stem: The capital of the Sokoto Caliphate, founded in 1809, was built by
questions.explanation:
Muhammad Bello, Usman's son, founded Sokoto in 1809 and became caliph after Usman's death in 1817.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Abdullahi: Abdullahi, Usman's brother, ruled the western emirates from Gwandu.
- Yunfa: Yunfa was the king of Gobir defeated by the jihadists.
- Ahmadu Seku: Ahmadu Seku was al-Hajj Umar's son, ruling from Segou.

questions.stem: Al-Hajj Umar Tall belonged to which Islamic brotherhood?
questions.explanation:
Al-Hajj Umar was made khalifa of the Tijaniyya brotherhood for West Africa during his pilgrimage to Mecca.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Qadiriyya: Usman dan Fodio belonged to the Qadiriyya, the older brotherhood.
- the Mouride: The Mouride brotherhood was founded later in Senegal by Amadou Bamba.
- the Sanusiyya: The Sanusiyya was a Libyan brotherhood.

questions.stem: One political effect of the nineteenth-century jihads was the
questions.explanation:
The jihads created large states such as Sokoto, Masina and the Tukulor empire, destroyed older states, spread Islam and learning, but also caused wars and slave raiding.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- immediate colonisation of Hausaland by France: Northern Nigeria was conquered by Britain in 1903, long after the jihad.
- revival of the Oyo empire: The jihad helped to destroy Old Oyo through Ilorin.
- end of Islam in the Western Sudan: The jihads spread and strengthened Islam.

options.label: A
options.content: immediate colonisation of Hausaland by France

options.label: B
options.content: creation of large new states such as the Sokoto Caliphate

options.label: D
options.content: end of Islam in the Western Sudan

papers.title: The European Partition of Africa: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the european partition of africa, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 was called by
questions.explanation:
The German chancellor Otto von Bismarck called the Berlin Conference to agree rules for claiming African territory without war between European powers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- King Leopold II: Leopold II benefited from the conference but did not call it.
- Cecil Rhodes: Cecil Rhodes was a British imperialist in southern Africa.
- Frederick Lugard: Lugard was a British colonial administrator in Nigeria.

questions.stem: The principle of 'effective occupation' agreed at Berlin meant that a European power must
questions.explanation:
A power claiming coastal territory had to occupy it effectively, with an administration able to keep order and protect trade, and notify other powers.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- obtain the consent of the African people by referendum: Africans were not consulted at Berlin.
- buy the land from the Ottoman Empire: There was no such rule.
- leave Africa within ten years: The conference was about claiming Africa, not leaving it.

options.label: A
options.content: obtain the consent of the African people by referendum

options.label: B
options.content: buy the land from the Ottoman Empire

options.label: D
options.content: set up a real administration in coastal territory it claimed

questions.stem: Which of the following was an economic cause of the Scramble for Africa?
questions.explanation:
European industries needed raw materials such as palm oil, rubber and cotton, protected markets and places to invest, especially during the depression of 1873–96.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the Haitian Revolution: The Haitian Revolution influenced abolition, not the Scramble.
- the spread of the camel caravans: Camel caravans belong to the trans-Saharan trade.
- the decline of Timbuktu's scholars: This had no link with European economic motives.

options.label: A
options.content: the need for raw materials and markets for European industries

options.label: C
options.content: the spread of the camel caravans

questions.stem: Which two African countries were still independent in 1914?
questions.explanation:
By 1914 only Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at Adwa in 1896, and Liberia remained independent.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Egypt and Morocco: Egypt was under British and Morocco under French control.
- Ghana and Nigeria: Both were British colonies until 1957 and 1960.
- Sierra Leone and Senegal: Sierra Leone was British and Senegal French.

questions.stem: Which effect of the partition explains why the Ewe people live in both Ghana and Togo?
questions.explanation:
Colonial borders were drawn by European agreements, often splitting peoples such as the Ewe (Ghana and Togo), Yoruba (Nigeria and Benin) and Hausa (Nigeria and Niger).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the spread of Islam by the jihads: The jihads did not divide the Ewe.
- the trans-Saharan caravan routes: The caravan routes did not create modern borders.
- the voluntary migration of Ewe to Europe: There was no such migration.

options.label: A
options.content: the spread of Islam by the jihads

options.label: C
options.content: artificial boundaries drawn without regard to African peoples

options.label: D
options.content: the voluntary migration of Ewe to Europe

papers.title: Systems of Colonial Administration: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on systems of colonial administration, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Indirect rule is most closely associated with
questions.explanation:
Lugard developed indirect rule in Northern Nigeria after 1900, ruling through the emirs under British Residents.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Blaise Diagne in Senegal: Blaise Diagne was the first Black African deputy in the French parliament.
- Frederic Cardew in Sierra Leone: Cardew introduced the hut tax in Sierra Leone.
- Félix Éboué in Chad: Éboué was a French colonial governor who joined the Free French.

questions.stem: Indirect rule failed in Eastern Nigeria mainly because
questions.explanation:
Igbo and other eastern societies were decentralised; the warrant chiefs the British appointed had no traditional authority, were often corrupt, and the Aba Women's War of 1929 followed.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the emirs refused to collect taxes: The emirs were in the North, where indirect rule worked.
- the French controlled Eastern Nigeria: Eastern Nigeria was British.
- there were too many British officials: Indirect rule was used because there were too few officials.

options.label: A
options.content: most societies there had no kings, so the British created warrant chiefs

options.label: B
options.content: the emirs refused to collect taxes

options.label: D
options.content: there were too many British officials

questions.stem: The Four Communes of Senegal, whose people were French citizens, were Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque and
questions.explanation:
Assimilation was applied fully only in the Four Communes of Senegal: Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque and Dakar.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Bamako: Bamako is in Mali, not one of the Four Communes.
- Conakry: Conakry is the capital of Guinea.
- Abidjan: Abidjan is in Côte d'Ivoire.

questions.stem: The indigénat in French West Africa was
questions.explanation:
Under the indigénat, French officials could fine or imprison African subjects without trial; it and forced labour were abolished in 1946.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a council of traditional rulers: French chiefs were appointed agents, not a ruling council.
- the French name for indirect rule: The French used direct rule, not indirect rule.
- a school for training évolués: The indigénat was a legal code of punishments.

options.label: B
options.content: the French name for indirect rule

options.label: C
options.content: a code allowing officials to punish African subjects without trial

questions.stem: A major difference between British and French colonial rule was that
questions.explanation:
Under indirect rule, traditional rulers kept authority as Native Authorities; under French direct rule, chiefs were appointed, moved or dismissed as civil servants.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Britain used forced labour while France never did: France used forced labour (corvée) widely until 1946.
- France allowed no African deputies in Paris: The Four Communes elected deputies to the French parliament.
- Britain governed all its colonies as one federation: French West Africa was a federation; British colonies were separate.

options.label: A
options.content: Britain used forced labour while France never did

options.label: B
options.content: France allowed no African deputies in Paris

options.label: C
options.content: Britain governed all its colonies as one federation

options.label: D
options.content: British rule kept traditional rulers in power, while the French made chiefs appointed agents

papers.title: Resistance to Colonial Rule: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on resistance to colonial rule, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Samori Toure resisted which European power?
questions.explanation:
Samori Toure resisted French conquest from 1882 until his capture at Guelemou in 1898.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Britain: Samori sought British help; his long war was against the French.
- Germany: Germany had no colonies in Samori's region.
- Portugal: Portugal held only Guinea-Bissau, not Samori's lands.

questions.stem: One reason Samori Toure resisted the French for so long was that he
questions.explanation:
Samori had a strong standing army, bought and made guns, used scorched-earth tactics, moved his empire east, and used diplomacy to gain time.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- received military help from the British: Britain refused to help or sell him arms.
- had more Maxim guns than the French: The French had superior weapons.
- signed no treaties with the French: He signed the treaties of Kenieba-Koura and Bissandugu.

options.label: A
options.content: received military help from the British

options.label: B
options.content: used scorched-earth tactics and moved his empire eastwards

options.label: C
options.content: had more Maxim guns than the French

options.label: D
options.content: signed no treaties with the French

questions.stem: Jaja of Opobo came into conflict with the British mainly because he
questions.explanation:
Jaja controlled the palm-oil markets of the interior and blocked British traders; Consul Johnston arrested and deported him in 1887.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- led a jihad against Christian missionaries: Jaja's conflict was commercial, not religious.
- refused to hand over the Golden Stool: The Golden Stool was the issue in Asante in 1900.
- opposed the hut tax in Sierra Leone: The hut tax war was in Sierra Leone in 1898.

options.label: A
options.content: led a jihad against Christian missionaries

options.label: B
options.content: refused to hand over the Golden Stool

options.label: C
options.content: held a monopoly of the palm-oil trade and refused free trade

options.label: D
options.content: opposed the hut tax in Sierra Leone

questions.stem: The immediate cause of the Yaa Asantewaa War of 1900 was
questions.explanation:
In March 1900 Governor Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool so he could sit on it; Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, led the Asante war.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the introduction of the hut tax in Sierra Leone: That caused the Hut Tax War of 1898.
- the arrest of Jaja of Opobo: Jaja was arrested in 1887 in the Niger Delta.
- the Berlin Conference's decisions: The Berlin Conference set rules for partition in 1884–85.

options.label: A
options.content: the introduction of the hut tax in Sierra Leone

options.label: B
options.content: the arrest of Jaja of Opobo

options.label: D
options.content: the British Governor's demand for the Golden Stool

questions.stem: Which of the following was a general reason for the failure of African resistance?
questions.explanation:
Resistance failed because of superior European weapons, African disunity, African troops in European armies, European resources and diplomacy.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Africans had no armies at all: Many African states had large, organised armies.
- Europeans never used African soldiers: Europeans relied heavily on African troops.
- African rulers always united against Europeans: African disunity helped Europeans conquer.

options.label: A
options.content: Europeans had superior weapons such as the Maxim gun

options.label: B
options.content: Africans had no armies at all

options.label: D
options.content: African rulers always united against Europeans

papers.topic: Nationalism and the Road to Independence
papers.title: Nationalism and the Road to Independence: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on nationalism and the road to independence, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The National Congress of British West Africa (NCBWA) was founded in 1920 under the leadership of
questions.explanation:
The NCBWA was founded in Accra in March 1920 by educated Africans from all four British West African colonies, led by J. E. Casely Hayford.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Kwame Nkrumah: Nkrumah led the CPP from 1949.
- Nnamdi Azikiwe: Azikiwe founded the West African Pilot (1937) and co-founded the NCNC.
- Milton Margai: Milton Margai led the SLPP from 1951.

questions.stem: Which of the following was a cause of the growth of nationalism in West Africa after 1945?
questions.explanation:
Ex-servicemen, the Atlantic Charter, the UN, India's independence, economic hardship and mass parties turned nationalism into a mass movement after 1945.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the founding of Elmina Castle: Elmina was built in 1482.
- the Moroccan invasion of Songhai: That happened in 1591.
- the decline of the trans-Saharan trade: This was not a cause of modern nationalism.

options.label: C
options.content: the return of African ex-servicemen from the Second World War

options.label: D
options.content: the decline of the trans-Saharan trade

questions.stem: Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957 under the leadership of
questions.explanation:
Kwame Nkrumah's Convention People's Party (1949) led the Gold Coast to independence as Ghana on 6 March 1957.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- J. B. Danquah: Danquah led the UGCC, which Nkrumah left in 1949.
- Sékou Touré: Sékou Touré led Guinea to independence in 1958.
- Obafemi Awolowo: Awolowo led the Action Group in Western Nigeria.

questions.stem: Guinea became independent in 1958 because it
questions.explanation:
In the 1958 referendum, only Guinea, led by Ahmed Sékou Touré, voted 'No' to joining the French Community and became independent on 2 October 1958.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- won a long war of liberation against France: Guinea's independence came by referendum, not war.
- was a British colony that followed Ghana: Guinea was a French colony.
- was given independence at the Berlin Conference: The Berlin Conference divided Africa among Europeans.

options.label: A
options.content: voted 'No' in de Gaulle's referendum on the French Community

options.label: B
options.content: won a long war of liberation against France

options.label: C
options.content: was a British colony that followed Ghana

options.label: D
options.content: was given independence at the Berlin Conference

questions.stem: Which Sierra Leonean founded the West African Youth League?
questions.explanation:
Wallace-Johnson founded the West African Youth League in the Gold Coast in 1935 and its Sierra Leone branch in 1938.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- H. C. Bankole-Bright: Bankole-Bright was an NCBWA delegate and later led the NCSL.
- Siaka Stevens: Stevens was a trade unionist who later founded the APC.
- Samuel Lewis: Sir Samuel Lewis was Freetown's first mayor in 1895.

papers.title: Pan-Africanism: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on pan-africanism, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The first Pan-African Conference, held in London in 1900, was organised by
questions.explanation:
The Trinidadian lawyer Henry Sylvester Williams organised the first Pan-African Conference in London in 1900.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Marcus Garvey: Garvey founded the UNIA in 1914.
- George Padmore: Padmore helped organise the Manchester Congress of 1945.
- Edward Blyden: Blyden was an early thinker of the 'African personality', not the 1900 organiser.

questions.stem: Marcus Garvey is associated with the slogan
questions.explanation:
Marcus Garvey, the Jamaican founder of the UNIA, preached 'Africa for the Africans' and racial pride.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 'Self-government now': 'Self-government now' was the slogan of Nkrumah's CPP.
- 'One Country, One People': That was the SLPP's motto in Sierra Leone.
- 'Elections before peace': That was the demand at Bintumani II in Sierra Leone in 1996.

questions.stem: Why was the Manchester Pan-African Congress of 1945 a turning point?
questions.explanation:
At Manchester, leaders such as Nkrumah and Kenyatta demanded independence and supported mass action, and then went home to lead independence movements.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- it created the African Union: The AU was launched in 2002.
- it was the first meeting held in Africa: The first major Pan-African meeting in Africa was in Accra in 1958.
- it divided Africa among European powers: That was the Berlin Conference of 1884–85.

options.label: A
options.content: Africans from Africa dominated it and demanded full independence

options.label: C
options.content: it was the first meeting held in Africa

options.label: D
options.content: it divided Africa among European powers

questions.stem: The Organisation of African Unity was founded on 25 May 1963 at
questions.explanation:
Thirty-two independent states founded the OAU at Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, on 25 May 1963, now celebrated as Africa Day.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Accra: Accra hosted the All-African Peoples' Conference in 1958.
- Durban: The African Union was launched at Durban in 2002.
- Lagos: ECOWAS was founded by the Treaty of Lagos in 1975.

questions.stem: A major weakness of the OAU was its principle of
questions.explanation:
Non-interference stopped the OAU from acting against dictators, coups and civil wars; the AU later gained the right to intervene in genocide and war crimes.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- support for liberation movements: Support for liberation was one of its achievements.
- respect for colonial borders: Accepting borders helped to prevent border wars.
- opposition to apartheid: Opposition to apartheid was one of its achievements.

options.label: C
options.content: non-interference in the internal affairs of member states

papers.title: Africa in the 20th Century: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on africa in the 20th century, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: After the First World War, Germany's African colonies became
questions.explanation:
Togoland and Kamerun were divided between Britain and France, Tanganyika went to Britain, Ruanda-Urundi to Belgium and South West Africa to South Africa, as mandates.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- independent states: They were placed under other colonial powers, not made independent.
- parts of French West Africa: Only parts of Togoland and Kamerun went to France, as mandates.
- members of the Commonwealth: The Commonwealth of independent states came later.

questions.stem: The Atlantic Charter of 1941 encouraged African nationalism because it
questions.explanation:
The Atlantic Charter declared the right of all peoples to choose the form of government under which they live, which African nationalists claimed for themselves.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ended the slave trade in Africa: The slave trade had been abolished long before.
- created the Organisation of African Unity: The OAU was founded in 1963.
- divided Africa among the Allies: The Charter did not divide Africa.

options.label: A
options.content: spoke of the right of all peoples to choose their own government

options.label: B
options.content: ended the slave trade in Africa

options.label: C
options.content: created the Organisation of African Unity

questions.stem: Why is 1960 called the 'Year of Africa'?
questions.explanation:
In 1960 seventeen African countries, including Nigeria and most French colonies, became independent.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the OAU was founded that year: The OAU was founded in 1963.
- apartheid ended that year: Apartheid ended with the 1994 election.
- the Berlin Conference was held that year: The Berlin Conference was in 1884–85.

options.label: A
options.content: the OAU was founded that year

options.label: B
options.content: seventeen African countries became independent that year

options.label: D
options.content: the Berlin Conference was held that year

questions.stem: Apartheid in South Africa was introduced by the National Party after it won power in
questions.explanation:
The National Party won the 1948 election and introduced apartheid laws such as the Population Registration Act and the Group Areas Act (1950).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- 1910: 1910 was when the Union of South Africa was formed.
- 1960: 1960 was the year of the Sharpeville massacre.
- 1994: 1994 was the year apartheid ended with the first non-racial election.

questions.stem: ECOWAS was founded in 1975 by the
questions.explanation:
The Economic Community of West African States was founded by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975, with fifteen founding members.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Treaty of Abuja: The Abuja Treaty of 1991 planned an African Economic Community.
- Lomé Peace Agreement: The Lomé Agreement of 1999 concerned Sierra Leone's civil war.
- Constitutive Act: The Constitutive Act (2000) created the African Union.
